g.text: Why state must persist — and why it is only a cache
7 entries for 9 events · restart replays 9 without a checkpoint, 4 with one
seed: tools/stream_seed.js · 7 state entries · total 45
WHAT THE PROCESSOR IS HOLDING — ONE ENTRY PER (KEY, WINDOW)
7 entries for 9 events — this is the whole of "state"
8 (from ids 0, 1)
11 (from ids 2, 7)
2 (from ids 3)
6 (from ids 4)
1 (from ids 5)
9 (from ids 6)
8 (from ids 8)
Nothing mysterious: state is 7 numbers, each the partial sum of a (key, window) group that has not finished yet.
Without it every event would start from zero, so the pipeline could not compute anything that spans more than one record.
Step 1/4 — state is the aggregation in progress
Worth making concrete before discussing how to persist it: the state here is 7 numbers. Each one is a partial aggregate for a (key, window) group
that is still open. Everything in this chapter — checkpoints, state stores, barriers — exists to move those 7 numbers safely across a restart.
Why state must persist — and why it is only a cache
7 entries for 9 events · restart replays 9 without a checkpoint, 4 with one
seed: tools/stream_seed.js · 7 state entries · total 45
RECOVERY COST, WITH AND WITHOUT PERSISTED STATE
persistence buys recovery time, not correctness
no persisted state
re-read all 9 events to rebuild 7 entries
state persisted at event 4
re-read 4 events — the ones after the checkpoint
the reduction
9 → 4 reads, and it grows with the stream
both are CORRECT
the difference is entirely cost — the stream is the truth either way
The last row is the one to keep. A full reprocess gives the right answer; it just takes as long as the history is.
So persisted state is a CACHE of a fold over the stream. You can always throw it away, and on a long stream you cannot afford to.
Step 2/4 — and a restart without it re-reads the whole stream
The honest framing: persistence is an optimisation, not a correctness mechanism. Rebuilding from the stream gives exactly the same 7 entries — it
just reads 9 events instead of 4. On a nine-event stream that is nothing; on a year of history it is the difference between a minute and a week.
Why state must persist — and why it is only a cache
7 entries for 9 events · restart replays 9 without a checkpoint, 4 with one
seed: tools/stream_seed.js · 7 state entries · total 45
WHAT CAN BE REBUILT FROM WHAT
the derivation runs one way, which is what makes the stream primary
the stream
9 events, total 45 — the source of truth
the state
7 entries — a fold over a PREFIX of the stream
stream → state
always possible: replay and re-fold
state → stream
NOT possible: the 7 partial sums do not name the events
This is ch06's duality applied to recovery: the state is a materialized fold, and the fold is not invertible for a sum over multiple events.
Which is why losing the state is survivable and losing the stream is not.
Step 3/4 — so the state store is a cache, and the stream is the truth
The asymmetry decides the architecture. Entry `a@0` holds 8, which came from 2 events — and from 8 alone you cannot say which. So state is
recoverable from the stream and the stream is not recoverable from state, which is the whole reason the stream is retained.
Why state must persist — and why it is only a cache
7 entries for 9 events · restart replays 9 without a checkpoint, 4 with one
seed: tools/stream_seed.js · 7 state entries · total 45
WHEN EACH ENTRY CAN BE DROPPED
the watermark is what makes state collectable, and therefore bounded
a @ window 0
after event 4, when the watermark reaches 12:03:05
b @ window 0
after event 4, when the watermark reaches 12:03:05
a @ window 120
after event 8, when the watermark reaches 12:08:00
a @ window 240
after event 8, when the watermark reaches 12:08:00
b @ window 240
after event 8, when the watermark reaches 12:08:00
b @ window 120
after event 8, when the watermark reaches 12:08:00
a @ window 480
NEVER — the watermark never passes its end
1 of the 7 entries is never collectable in this stream, so its 8 is held for the life of the job.
A window that never closes is an allocation that never ends. That is the failure mode persistence makes permanent rather than transient.
Step 4/4 — and the bound on it is the watermark
State is bounded only by the watermark, and this stream shows the gap: 6 entries become collectable and 1 does not, because no event ever pushes
the watermark past window [12:08, …). Persisting state makes that leak survive restarts, which turns a transient memory problem into a permanent
one.
